content: Alcoholic hepatitis is a condition caused by excessive alcohol consumption. Approximately 2% of adults suffer from alcohol use disorder. The symptoms of alcoholic hepatitis can range from mild to severe. Therefore, any patient suspected of having this condition should undergo liver function tests and an ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis. If left untreated, alcoholic hepatitis can progress to hepatic steatonecrosis, fibrosis, cirrhosis, or hepatocellular carcinoma. As a result, all patients must be strongly advised to abstain from alcohol. Nutritional supplements, including folic acid, thiamine, vitamin B6, vitamin A, and zinc, may also be provided to support recovery. In cases where alcoholic hepatitis progresses to cirrhosis, liver transplantation may be considered as a treatment option. Alcoholic hepatitis was first recognized in 1961 after the investigation of seven cases involving excessive alcohol intake. Before this recognition, it was believed that the symptoms were primarily caused by malnutrition rather than the toxic effects of alcohol. Charles S. Lieber was instrumental in developing modern research on alcohol-related liver disease. The pathophysiology of alcoholic hepatitis involves a complex interplay between alcohol metabolism, inflammation, and innate immunity. Alcohol metabolism depletes NAD, leading to lipogenesis. Additionally, increased endotoxemia results in the translocation of lipopolysaccharides from the intestine to hepatocytes. Within hepatocytes, lipopolysaccharides activate Kupffer cells, which then release inflammatory markers that contribute to the development of alcoholic hepatitis. Alcohol is the primary cause of alcoholic hepatitis. Other associated factors include hepatitis C and malnutrition. It is essential to differentiate alcoholic hepatitis from other liver diseases, such as viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, drug-induced liver injury, Wilson disease, cholestatic liver diseases, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Women are at a higher risk of developing alcoholic hepatitis after shorter durations and smaller amounts of alcohol intake compared to men. The most common risk factors for developing alcoholic hepatitis include heavy alcohol intake, high body mass index, female gender, malnutrition, and hepatitis C. Patients with excessive alcohol consumption should be screened for alcohol use disorder using the AUDIT questionnaire. A score above 8 indicates alcohol use disorder, necessitating further evaluation with liver tests and ultrasound. Alcoholic liver disease can progress through various stages, including fatty liver, hepatic steatosis, alcoholic hepatitis, alcoholic steatonecrosis, fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Complications of alcoholic hepatitis include variceal hemorrhage, hepatic encephalopathy, ascites, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and iron overload. Prognosis and mortality among patients with alcoholic hepatitis can be predicted using scoring systems, with the Asymmetric Dimethylarginine (ADMA) score being the most recent and accurate. Symptoms of alcoholic hepatitis include nausea, malaise, low-grade fever, abdominal pain, jaundice, increased abdominal girth due to ascites, gastrointestinal bleeding from variceal hemorrhage, loss of appetite, confusion, and lethargy. Physical examination findings in alcoholic hepatitis may include fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, respiratory alkalosis, hepatomegaly, hepatic tenderness, scleral icterus, splenomegaly, ascites, asterixis, dark urine, peripheral edema, gynecomastia, palmar erythema, spider angiomas, altered hair distribution, and proximal muscle wasting. Laboratory findings commonly observed in alcoholic hepatitis include neutrophilic leukocytosis with bandemia, anemia, an AST/ALT ratio greater than 2, mild elevation of alkaline phosphatase, hypoalbuminemia, hyperbilirubinemia, prolonged prothrombin time, and elevated gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase levels. There are no specific X-ray findings associated with alcoholic hepatitis. However, CT scans can help predict the severity and outcome of the disease by identifying features such as splenomegaly, ascites, varices, liver length to midclavicular line, decreased liver attenuation, liver-to-spleen attenuation ratio, and increased liver heterogeneity. MRI findings in alcoholic hepatitis are non-specific and are typically used to exclude other etiologies. These findings may include hepatic steatosis, increased T2 signal around the portal system, and increased parenchymal signal intensity. Ultrasound is the preferred imaging modality for alcoholic hepatitis. Findings may include hepatomegaly, irregular liver surface and edge nodularity, diffuse hyperechoic liver, and atrophy of the right lobe. Additional features such as splenomegaly and varices may suggest portal hypertension. Liver biopsy is indicated in cases where the diagnosis is uncertain or in patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis who are likely to undergo medical treatment. Histological findings in alcoholic hepatitis include polymorphonuclear infiltration, hepatic necrosis, Mallory bodies in hepatocytes, perivenular and perisinusoidal fibrosis, ballooning hepatocytes, and steatosis. All patients with alcoholic hepatitis must be advised to cease alcohol consumption. Nutritional supplementation with folic acid, thiamine, vitamin B6, vitamin A, and zinc may be provided. Glucocorticoids are the most commonly used pharmacologic treatment for alcoholic hepatitis, while pentoxifylline may be used in patients with contraindications to steroids. Liver transplantation is considered in cases of cirrhosis. Orthotopic liver transplantation is the definitive surgical treatment for hepatic failure associated with alcoholic hepatitis. A six-month period of alcohol abstinence is required before transplantation. Alcohol abstinence improves histological features of hepatic injury, reduces portal hypertension, and lowers the risk of cirrhosis. However, the risk of recidivism after abstinence is 67% to 81%. Therefore, a combination of psychotherapy, cognitive behavioral therapy, peer-driven support counseling, motivational enhancement therapy, and comprehensive medical care is recommended. Additionally, medications such as baclofen and gamma-hydroxybutyrate may help reduce recidivism in patients with advanced chronic liver disease.
